questions.q: Why does this lesson compare a static API key shared between two services to a flat, unsegmented network?
options: Both are long-lived, often location-independent, all-or-nothing credentials or paths that grant broad access once compromised
Because API keys and network segments use the same encryption algorithm
Because flat networks are only a problem for human users, not services
Because static API keys automatically expire every few minutes, just like a segmented network path
questions.explain: A static API key, once leaked, grants the full privilege of the service it represents indefinitely from almost anywhere — the same shape of risk a flat network creates at the network layer.

questions.q: What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add beyond ordinary TLS?
options: It removes the need for certificates entirely
It only encrypts the connection, with no identity verification on either side
Both the client and the server present and verify certificates, so each side proves its identity to the other, not just the server to the client
It replaces OAuth2 tokens as the only credential a service ever needs
questions.explain: Ordinary TLS proves only the server's identity to the client. Mutual TLS requires both sides to present and verify certificates, so a calling service must cryptographically prove its own identity too.

questions.q: In a service mesh architecture, what role does the sidecar proxy play?
options: It stores the application's business logic so the main service container can be removed
It is only used for logging and has no role in authentication
It replaces the need for any policy enforcement point described earlier in the course
It intercepts a service's inbound and outbound traffic, handling the mTLS handshake, certificate rotation, and service-to-service policy enforcement
questions.explain: The sidecar proxy does the identity and policy work outside the application's own code, so the application never has to manage private keys or rotation schedules directly.

questions.q: What advantage does a short-lived, OAuth2 client-credentials-style token have over a static API key baked into configuration?
options: It never needs to be scoped to specific permissions
It is minted fresh and expires quickly, so a leaked token is already close to useless by the time it could be exploited
It is valid indefinitely once issued, same as a static key
It eliminates the need for the calling service to authenticate to a token issuer at all
questions.explain: Short-lived tokens are scoped to the specific operation and expire in minutes rather than months, dramatically shrinking the exploitation window if one leaks.

questions.q: What two complementary layers does this lesson describe for securing a service-to-service call?
options: A static API key and a shared password, used together for redundancy
Network segmentation alone, with no identity verification needed at the application layer
Mutual TLS, which proves which service is calling, and a short-lived token, which proves what that service is authorized to do on this call
A single long-lived certificate that never needs to be verified again after the first connection
questions.explain: mTLS establishes cryptographic proof of identity at the transport layer; a short-lived, scoped token then authorizes the specific action for that call — together they replace a single static API key.
